L2S42.title: Game feel and juice

blockRefs.what: Changes a visual effect such as colour or ghost.
blockRefs.tip: Fun for power-ups and flashing damage.

blockRefs.what: Plays a sound and carries straight on with the code.
blockRefs.tip: Use this for game effects so the action isn't paused.

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite bigger or smaller by an amount.
blockRefs.tip: Grow-then-shrink makes a satisfying 'pop' effect.

blockRefs.what: Sends a message that every sprite can hear.
blockRefs.tip: Name messages properly — 'game-over', never 'message1'.

vocab: Game feel — how satisfying a game is to play.
Juice — small effects that make actions feel good.
Playtest — watching someone else play to find problems.
objectives: I can add feedback to every player action.
I can improve a game after watching someone play it.
I can explain what makes a game feel good.
L2S42.hook: Play the same action with and without sound, shake and pop. Ask which feels better. Polish is not decoration — it is communication.
teach: List every player action in their game (move, collect, hit, win). Each one needs feedback: sound, animation or effect.
Add a collect effect together: sound plus a quick grow-and-fade. Small work, large payoff.
Playtest properly: the tutor plays while the CHILD watches silently and writes down every confusion. Not explaining is the hard part — and the lesson.
Fix the top two issues found. Real iteration.
watch: Child adds effects everywhere until it is chaotic → one clear effect per action.
Child explains the game while it is being tested → the game must speak for itself.
Feedback ignored because 'it's fine' → pick just the single most common confusion and fix that.
ask: What is game feel? → How satisfying the game is to play.
What did your playtester find confusing? → (child's own answer)
Why watch silently? → Because a real player has nobody to explain it.
L2S42.support: Add feedback to one action together and let the child mirror it for the rest.
L2S42.stretch: Run two playtests and produce a prioritised fix list.

rubric.secure: Gives every action clear feedback and acts on playtest findings.
rubric.mastered: Iterates deliberately on feel and justifies design choices.

Fix the top two issues found. Real iteration.
watch: Child adds effects everywhere until it is chaotic → one clear effect per action.
Child explains the game while it is being tested → the game must speak for itself.
Feedback ignored because 'it's fine' → pick just the single most common confusion and fix that.
ask: What is game feel? → How satisfying the game is to play.
What did your playtester find confusing? → (child's own answer)
Why watch silently? → Because a real player has nobody to explain it.

L2S44.title: Advanced debugging

blockRefs.what: Stops the whole project.
blockRefs.tip: Say your message BEFORE stopping, or nobody can read it.

blockRefs.what: Shows a speech bubble that stays until you change it.
blockRefs.tip: It never disappears on its own — clear it with an empty say.

blockRefs.what: Pauses this script for a time.
blockRefs.tip: Use 0.1 or 0.2 for smooth animation, 1 for conversations.

vocab: Bug — a mistake that makes a program behave wrongly.
Debug — to find and fix a bug.
Test — to run code deliberately to see what happens.
objectives: I can describe what a program does wrongly.
I can find the block causing a bug.
I can fix a bug and re-test.
L2S44.hook: Say: "Every professional programmer's code is broken most of the day. Finding bugs is the actual job — and you're about to be good at it." This reframes failure permanently.
teach: Give the child a project you have broken on purpose. Ask first: what SHOULD it do, and what does it do instead? Naming the gap is step one.
Teach the three moves: (1) run it and watch closely, (2) click a single script to test it alone, (3) add a `say` to see what the code thinks is happening.
Slow it down with waits so the failure becomes visible.
Fix it, then re-run to confirm. Insist on the re-test — fixing without verifying is a habit worth preventing early.
watch: Child changes many things at once → change ONE thing, then test. Otherwise you cannot tell what worked.
Child deletes the whole script in frustration → encourage isolating instead; keep a copy first.
Child assumes the computer is wrong → the computer does exactly what it was told; find what it was told.
ask: What is a bug? → A mistake making the program behave wrongly.
What is the first thing to do? → Say what it should do versus what it does.
Why change one thing at a time? → So you know which change fixed it.
L2S44.support: Debug together, thinking aloud so the child hears your reasoning; then let them lead the next one.
L2S44.stretch: Give a project with two independent bugs and ask them to log what they tried.

rubric.emerging: Spots that something is wrong but not where.
rubric.secure: Isolates and fixes a bug, then re-tests.
rubric.mastered: Debugs systematically, one change at a time, and explains the cause.

L2S45.title: Publishing your work
vocab: Publish — make a project visible to others.
Instructions — telling a player how to play.
Credits — acknowledging work you have used.
Remix — building on someone else's shared project.
objectives: I can write clear instructions for my project.
I can credit the work of others.
I can share a project and respond to feedback.
L2S45.hook: Ask: "You open a game and there are no instructions. What do you do?" Quit. Instructions are part of the game.
teach: Write the Instructions field together: how to play in three lines, no jargon.
Write Notes and Credits: what they made, what they reused, who helped. Attribution is an ethics lesson worth having early.
Discuss online safety: no real names, no school, no personal details in a public project.
Share the project and send the link to a parent — the moment the work becomes real.
watch: Instructions assume the player already knows → test them on someone who has never seen the game.
No credits for reused sprites or sounds → add them; it is good practice and good manners.
Personal details in the project → remove them and explain why.
ask: What three things do instructions need? → Goal, controls, how to win.
Why credit others? → It is honest and respectful of their work.
What should never go in a public project? → Personal details.
L2S45.support: Draft the instructions together sentence by sentence.
L2S45.stretch: Ask them to remix someone else's shared project and credit it properly.

L2S46.title: Capstone: write the spec
vocab: Specification — a written description of what will be built.
Milestone — a checkpoint in a bigger build.
Portfolio — a collection of work that shows your skill.
objectives: I can specify a multi-feature project.

L2S46.hook: Say: "This is the project you'll show people. Make it something you'd actually want to play."
teach: Write a one-page spec: title, goal, controls, three features, win and lose conditions. Agree it before any code.
Break it into milestones and build one per session, testing each. Managing a build over time is the real Level 2 skill.
Require at least three Level 2 techniques (clones, broadcasts, custom blocks, lists or physics).
Finish with a presentation: demo, explain one clever piece of code, and say what was hardest and how they solved it.
watch: Scope far too large → cut to three features; a finished game beats an ambitious unfinished one.

Child stops testing near the end → test after every milestone, without exception.
ask: What are your three features? → (child's own answer)

Which Level 2 technique are you using and why? → (child's own answer)

L2S46.stretch: Add a stretch feature such as a level system, saved high scores or a boss.

move () steps.what: Moves the sprite forwards in the direction it is facing.
move () steps.tip: One step is about one dot on the screen — 10 is small, 100 is a big jump.

turn right () degrees.tip: 90 is a quarter turn, 180 is half, 360 is all the way round.

turn left () degrees.tip: Turning left 90 is the same as turning right 270.

turn () degrees.what: Turns the sprite by the number of degrees you choose.
turn () degrees.tip: Small turns inside a loop make smooth spinning.

point in direction ().what: Faces the sprite in an exact direction.
point in direction ().tip: 90 is right, -90 is left, 0 is up, 180 is down.

point towards ().what: Turns the sprite so it faces another sprite or the mouse.
point towards ().tip: Put it in a forever loop to keep watching a moving target.

point towards [mouse-pointer].what: Makes the sprite face wherever the mouse is.
point towards [mouse-pointer].tip: Great for eyes that follow you, or a turret that aims.

go to x: () y: ().what: Jumps the sprite instantly to an exact spot.
go to x: () y: ().tip: x 0, y 0 is the middle of the stage.

go to [random position].what: Jumps the sprite to a random spot on the stage.
go to [random position].tip: Perfect for making targets appear unpredictably.

go to [mouse-pointer].what: Makes the sprite sit exactly on the mouse.
go to [mouse-pointer].tip: The sprite will cover your pointer — offset it if that's a problem.

glide () secs to x: () y: ().what: Moves the sprite smoothly to a spot over a set time.
glide () secs to x: () y: ().tip: Use glide when you want the movement to be SEEN, not a teleport.

glide () secs to [random position].what: Glides smoothly to a random spot.
glide () secs to [random position].tip: Nice for fish, bees or ghosts drifting around.

change x by ().what: Moves the sprite left or right by an amount.
change x by ().tip: Negative numbers move left. This is how arrow-key movement works.

change y by ().what: Moves the sprite up or down by an amount.
change y by ().tip: Negative moves down — that's how falling works.

set x to ().what: Puts the sprite at an exact left/right position.
set x to ().tip: 'set' jumps there; 'change' moves by an amount. Very different!

x position.what: Reports how far left or right the sprite is.
x position.tip: Use it to check if a sprite has reached the edge.

y position.what: Reports how far up or down the sprite is.
y position.tip: Used for ground checks in jumping games.

if on edge, bounce.what: Turns the sprite around when it hits the edge of the stage.
if on edge, bounce.example: forever [move 10 steps, if on edge bounce]
if on edge, bounce.tip: Your sprite may go upside-down — fix it with rotation style left-right.

set rotation style ().what: Chooses how the sprite is allowed to rotate.
set rotation style ().tip: Use left-right to stop characters standing on their head.

say () for () seconds.what: Shows a speech bubble for a set time, then clears it.
say () for () seconds.tip: Use this one for conversations — it tidies up after itself.

say ().what: Shows a speech bubble that stays until you change it.
say ().tip: It never disappears on its own — clear it with an empty say.

think () for () seconds.what: Shows a thought bubble for a set time.
think () for () seconds.tip: Handy for showing what a character is feeling.

switch costume to ().what: Changes the sprite to a chosen picture.
switch costume to ().tip: Great for showing a state — walking, jumping, hurt.

next costume.what: Moves to the sprite's next picture.
next costume.tip: Without a wait it's a blur — animation needs timing.

costume number.what: Reports which costume the sprite is wearing.
costume number.tip: Useful for checking which state a sprite is in.

switch backdrop to ().tip: Backdrop code usually lives on the Stage, not a sprite.

next backdrop.tip: Good for flicking through scenes in a story.

when backdrop switches to ().what: Starts a script when the scene changes.

set size to () %.what: Sets the sprite's size, where 100% is normal.
set size to () %.tip: Always set size at the start so it resets every game.

change size by ().what: Makes the sprite bigger or smaller by an amount.

show.tip: Put this at the start — otherwise a hidden sprite stays invisible.

hide.tip: The classic bug: hiding a sprite and forgetting to show it next game.

change [ghost] effect by ().what: Makes the sprite more or less see-through.
change [ghost] effect by ().tip: 100 ghost = fully invisible. Great for fading out.

change () effect by ().what: Changes a visual effect such as colour or ghost.
change () effect by ().tip: Fun for power-ups and flashing damage.

clear graphic effects.tip: Add it at the start or last game's effects stay stuck on.

start sound ().what: Plays a sound and carries straight on with the code.
start sound ().tip: Use this for game effects so the action isn't paused.

play sound () until done.what: Plays a sound and waits for it to finish.
play sound () until done.tip: Use it when the next thing must not start too early.

stop all sounds.tip: Handy when the game ends or restarts.

change volume by ().what: Makes the sound louder or quieter.

when green flag clicked.what: Starts the script when the green flag is pressed.
when green flag clicked.tip: Every project needs one — it's how everything begins.

when [] key pressed.what: Starts the script when a key is pressed.
when [] key pressed.tip: Each key needs its own script.

when this sprite clicked.what: Starts the script when the player clicks this sprite.
when this sprite clicked.tip: Test by clicking the sprite on the STAGE, not in the sprite list.

broadcast ().what: Sends a message that every sprite can hear.

broadcast () and wait.what: Sends a message and waits until all receivers finish.
broadcast () and wait.tip: Use it when the next step must not start too soon.

when I receive ().what: Starts the script when a message is sent.
when I receive ().tip: One broadcast can start many sprites at once.

wait () seconds.what: Pauses this script for a time.
wait () seconds.tip: Use 0.1 or 0.2 for smooth animation, 1 for conversations.

wait until <>.tip: Great for 'don't start until the player is ready'.

repeat ().what: Repeats the blocks inside a set number of times.
repeat ().tip: Blocks must go INSIDE the C-shape, not underneath.

forever.what: Repeats the blocks inside for ever.
forever.tip: Nothing placed under a forever loop will ever run.

repeat until <>.tip: If the condition can never be true, the loop never stops.

if <> then.what: Runs the blocks inside only when something is true.
if <> then.tip: Usually needs a forever loop around it so it keeps checking.

if <> then else.what: Does one thing when true, a different thing when false.
if <> then else.tip: Use it when there are exactly two outcomes.

stop [all].tip: Say your message BEFORE stopping, or nobody can read it.

stop [this script].tip: Useful for ending one behaviour without ending the game.

when I start as a clone.key: when I start as a clone
when I start as a clone.what: Runs for each new clone that is made.
when I start as a clone.example: when I start as a clone [show, glide...]
when I start as a clone.tip: Each clone runs this separately with its own position.

create clone of ().what: Makes a copy of a sprite while the game runs.
create clone of ().tip: One sprite plus clones beats making 50 sprites by hand.

delete this clone.tip: Always delete clones when done or the project slows to a crawl.

touching ()?.what: Reports true when this sprite is touching another.
touching ()?.tip: Collision often fires many times a second — hide or wait to stop repeats.

touching color ()?.what: Reports true when the sprite touches a colour.
touching color ()?.tip: Pick the colour with the eyedropper — it must match exactly.

key () pressed?.what: Reports true while a key is held down.
key () pressed?.example: forever [if <key [right arrow] pressed?> then change x by 4]
key () pressed?.tip: Smoother than key events — no delay before it repeats.

distance to ().what: Reports how far away another sprite or the mouse is.
distance to ().tip: Great for 'enemy notices you when you get close'.

mouse x.tip: Use it for a paddle that slides side to side only.

mouse y.tip: Combine with mouse x to follow the pointer exactly.

ask () and wait.what: Asks the player a question and waits for them to type.
ask () and wait.tip: The reply goes into the 'answer' block.

answer.what: Holds whatever the player last typed.
answer.tip: The NEXT ask overwrites it — store it in a variable straight away.

timer.what: Reports how many seconds since the timer was reset.
timer.tip: Reset it at the start or it counts from when Scratch opened.

reset timer.what: Sets the timer back to zero.
reset timer.tip: Do this when the game starts so timing is fair.

() + ().tip: Green blocks go INSIDE other blocks' slots.

() - ().what: Takes one number away from another.
() - ().tip: Or use 'change lives by -1', which is shorter.

() * ().tip: Perfect for 'each coin is worth 10 points'.

() / ().tip: Can give long decimals — wrap it in 'round'.

round ().what: Rounds a number to the nearest whole number.

() < ().what: Reports true when the first number is smaller.
() < ().tip: Safer than '=' because values can skip past.

() = ().what: Reports true when two values are the same.
() = ().tip: For letters it ignores capitals, so 'paris' still matches.

() > ().what: Reports true when the first number is bigger.
() > ().tip: Use > instead of = for scores that jump by 2 or 5.

<> and <>.what: True only when BOTH conditions are true.
<> and <>.tip: Both must be true — like 'finish dinner AND tidy up'.

<> or <>.what: True when EITHER condition is true.
<> or <>.tip: Only one needs to be true.

not <>.what: Flips true into false and false into true.

join () ().what: Sticks two pieces of text together.
join () ().tip: Remember the space at the end of 'Hello ' or words run together.

pick random () to ().what: Gives a different random number each time.
pick random () to ().example: go to x: (pick random -200 to 200) y: 150
pick random () to ().tip: Keep x within -200..200 or your sprite lands off the stage.

set () to ().what: Puts an exact value into a variable.
set () to ().tip: Always reset score, lives and timers at the start of a game.

change () by ().what: Adds to what a variable already holds.
change () by ().tip: Use a negative number to take away.

show variable ().what: Shows the variable on the stage.
show variable ().tip: Players need to see the score to care about it.

hide variable ().what: Hides the variable from the stage.
hide variable ().tip: Hide working variables the player doesn't need to see.

add () to [].what: Adds an item to the end of a list.
add () to [].tip: Lists hold many values; a variable holds only one.

delete () of [].what: Removes one item from a list.
delete () of [].tip: 'delete all' clears the list — do that before refilling it.

item () of [].what: Reads the item at a position in a list.
item () of [].tip: Lists start at 1 in Scratch, not 0.

length of [].what: Reports how many items a list holds.
length of [].tip: This pattern picks a random item safely.

[] contains ()?.what: Reports true if the list holds a value.
[] contains ()?.tip: Handy for checking an answer against many possibilities.

define ().what: The script that says what your own block does.
define ().tip: Name it in plain English — 'reset player', not 'block1'.

custom block.what: A block you invented, used like any other block.
custom block.tip: Move repeated code here and your main script gets much clearer.

define () with inputs.what: Your own block that takes a value.
define () with inputs.tip: Drag the orange input from the hat into the blocks inside.

custom block with number input.what: Uses your block with a value you choose.
custom block with number input.tip: One block with an input beats five nearly identical blocks.

pen down.what: Starts drawing a line as the sprite moves.
pen down.tip: Needs the Pen extension, added from the bottom-left button.

pen up.tip: Lift the pen before moving into position, or you draw a stray line.

erase all.what: Clears everything drawn on the stage.
erase all.tip: Start every pen project with this or old drawings pile up.

set pen color to ().what: Chooses the colour to draw with.
set pen color to ().tip: Change it inside a loop for rainbow patterns.

set pen size to ().what: Chooses how thick the line is.
set pen size to ().tip: Thick lines for bold art, thin for detail.

change pen color by ().what: Shifts the pen colour a little.
change pen color by ().tip: This is how rainbow spirographs are made.

play drum () for () beats.what: Plays a drum sound for a number of beats.
play drum () for () beats.tip: Needs the Music extension. Put it in a loop to make a rhythm.

play note () for () beats.what: Plays a musical note for a number of beats.
play note () for () beats.tip: 60 is middle C. Higher numbers are higher notes.

set tempo to ().what: Sets how fast the music plays.

rest for () beats.what: A silent gap in the music.
rest for () beats.tip: Silence is part of rhythm — it's what makes a beat groove.

Motion.blurb: Move, turn and position your sprite.

Sensing.blurb: Detect touching, keys, the mouse and input.

Variables.blurb: Store scores, lives, timers and lists.

Pen.blurb: Draw on the stage as your sprite moves.

tour.stem: Where do you find the blocks you drag into your code?
options: The block palette on the left
The stage at the top right
tour.why: All the blocks live in the palette on the left, sorted into coloured groups.

options: A character or object you can give code to
tour.why: A sprite is a character or object. Each one has its own code, costumes and sounds.

tour.stem: What does the green flag do?
options: Runs every 'when green flag clicked' script
tour.why: The green flag is the usual way to start a project running.

tour.stem: Where does your project actually appear when it runs?
tour.why: The stage is the screen where everything you make is shown.

tour.stem: You added blocks but clicking the flag does nothing. What is most likely wrong?
options: There is no 'when green flag clicked' block on top
tour.why: Without a hat block listening for the flag, nothing tells the script to run.

options: A stack of blocks joined together
tour.why: A script is blocks snapped together so they run in order.

tour.stem: How do you know two blocks have joined properly?
options: They snap together with no gap
tour.why: Blocks snap together — if there is a gap, they are not connected and will not run in order.

tour.stem: You are editing code but it affects the wrong character. What should you check?
options: Which sprite is selected in the sprite list
tour.why: Code belongs to whichever sprite is selected, so always check the highlighted thumbnail.

tour.stem: What happens if you click a block on its own, without a hat block?
tour.why: Clicking a block or stack runs it immediately — a quick way to test an idea.

tour.stem: Which part of Scratch shows all your characters?
tour.why: The sprite list under the stage shows every sprite in your project.

options: Instructions carried out in order, one after another
Blocks that all run at the same time
sequence.why: A sequence means the order matters — each step runs after the one before it.

sequence.stem: If you swap two blocks in a script, what usually happens?
sequence.why: Order matters. Different order, different result.

options: A set of steps in order to get a job done
sequence.why: An algorithm is just a precise set of steps — a recipe for the computer.

sequence.stem: Your sprite does everything instantly and you cannot see the steps. What helps?
sequence.why: Waits slow the sequence down so you can actually watch each step happen.

sequence.stem: The blocks are: move 10, turn 90, move 10. Where does the sprite end up?
options: It moves, turns a quarter turn, then moves in the new direction
It moves 20 steps in a straight line
sequence.why: It moves, changes direction by 90 degrees, then moves along the NEW direction.

sequence.stem: Why should you predict what code will do before running it?
options: It helps you understand and spot mistakes
sequence.why: Predicting first turns running the code into a test of your thinking.

sequence.stem: Can two different orders of blocks reach the same end point?
options: Yes, often more than one algorithm works
No, only one order ever works
sequence.why: There is usually more than one way to solve a problem — that is real programming.

sequence.stem: Your sprite starts in the wrong place each time you run the project. What fixes it?
options: Add 'go to x: y:' at the start
sequence.why: Sprites keep their last position, so send them home at the start of every run.

sequence.stem: Why must instructions for a computer be precise?
options: The computer does exactly what you say, not what you mean
Precision is only needed in Level 2
sequence.why: A computer follows your instructions literally — vagueness produces bugs.

sequence.stem: Which is a sequence in real life?
options: Following a recipe step by step
sequence.why: A recipe is a sequence — the order of steps changes the result.

motion-steps.stem: How many degrees is a quarter turn?
motion-steps.why: 90 degrees is a quarter turn; 180 is half and 360 is a full circle.

options: Moves the sprite forwards in the direction it faces
Moves it 10 pixels to the right always
motion-steps.why: It moves forwards along whatever direction the sprite is currently pointing.

motion-steps.stem: You change 'move 10 steps' to 'move 100 steps'. What happens?
options: The sprite moves ten times further
motion-steps.why: The number controls the distance — bigger number, bigger jump.

motion-steps.stem: How could you make a sprite move backwards?
options: Use a negative number, like move -10 steps
motion-steps.why: Negative steps move the sprite in the opposite direction to where it faces.

motion-steps.stem: To draw a square path, which turn do you need each corner?
motion-steps.why: A square has four 90-degree corners: 4 x 90 = 360.

motion-steps.stem: To trace a triangle, what turn is needed at each corner?
motion-steps.why: 360 divided by 3 sides = 120 degrees per turn.

motion-steps.stem: Your sprite ends up upside-down after turning. What fixes it?
options: Set the rotation style to left-right
motion-steps.why: Rotation style controls whether a sprite is allowed to rotate all the way round.

motion-steps.stem: 'point in direction 90' makes the sprite face which way?
motion-steps.why: In Scratch 90 is right, -90 is left, 0 is up and 180 is down.

motion-steps.stem: Your sprite has moved off the stage and vanished. What can you do?
options: Drag it back, or add 'go to x: 0 y: 0'
motion-steps.why: Sending it to 0,0 brings it back to the centre of the stage.

motion-steps.stem: Which pair of blocks together makes a sprite follow a path with corners?
motion-steps.why: Moving then turning, repeated, traces a path with corners.

looks-say.stem: What is the difference between 'say Hello!' and 'say Hello! for 2 seconds'?
options: The timed one clears itself, the plain one stays forever
The timed one is bigger text
looks-say.why: 'say for seconds' tidies up after itself; plain 'say' leaves the bubble on screen.

looks-say.stem: How do you clear a speech bubble that will not go away?
options: Use a 'say' block with nothing in it
looks-say.why: An empty say block clears the bubble.

looks-say.stem: Two sprites talk over each other. What is the fix?
options: Give each a wait as long as the other's speech
looks-say.why: Matching waits to speaking time makes the sprites take turns properly.

looks-say.stem: Which block shows a thought bubble instead of speech?
looks-say.why: 'think' shows a thought cloud — good for showing what a character feels.

looks-say.stem: Sprite A says something for 2 seconds. How long should sprite B wait before replying?
looks-say.why: Sprite B should wait roughly as long as sprite A speaks, so they alternate.

options: Long text overflows and is hard to read
looks-say.why: Bubbles are small — keeping text short keeps it readable.

looks-say.stem: Which block would you use for a character greeting the player at the start?
looks-say.why: A timed say shows a greeting and then clears itself automatically.

looks-say.stem: What happens if two sprites both use plain 'say' with no waits?
options: Both bubbles appear at once and stay
looks-say.why: Without timing they speak simultaneously and neither bubble clears.

looks-say.stem: Where does a speech bubble appear?
options: Next to the sprite that said it
At the top of the stage
looks-say.why: The bubble belongs to the sprite that ran the block.

looks-say.stem: Which is the best way to build a conversation between two sprites?
options: Alternate say blocks with matching waits
Put all the says on one sprite
looks-say.why: Alternating speech with matching waits is how dialogue is timed in Scratch.

options: One of the pictures a sprite can wear
costumes.why: Costumes are the different pictures a sprite can switch between.

costumes.stem: How does switching costumes create animation?
options: The pictures swap quickly, like a flip-book
costumes.why: Animation is just pictures swapped fast enough to look like movement.

costumes.stem: Which block moves to the sprite's next picture?
costumes.why: 'next costume' steps to the following costume in the list.

costumes.stem: Your animation is a blur you cannot see. What is missing?
costumes.why: Without a small wait the costumes change too fast to see.

costumes.stem: Which tab do you use to see and edit a sprite's pictures?
costumes.why: The Costumes tab holds all of a sprite's pictures.

costumes.stem: You want a sprite to look hurt when hit. What is a good approach?
costumes.why: Costumes are perfect for showing a sprite's state, like hurt or jumping.

costumes.stem: How many costumes does a sprite need to look like it is walking?
costumes.why: Two alternating costumes already read as a walk cycle.

costumes.stem: What does the 'costume number' block report?
options: Which costume the sprite is currently wearing
costumes.why: It tells you the current costume, useful for checking a sprite's state.

costumes.stem: A good wait between costume changes for a walk is about:
costumes.why: Around 0.1-0.3 seconds looks like natural movement.

costumes.stem: Which block picks one exact picture rather than moving to the next?
costumes.why: 'switch costume to' jumps straight to the costume you name.

options: Runs the blocks inside it ten times
Runs the blocks below it ten times
animation-loop.why: A repeat loop runs whatever is INSIDE its C-shape, the set number of times.

animation-loop.stem: Why use a loop instead of copying the same blocks many times?
options: Less code and much easier to change
animation-loop.why: One loop replaces many copies, so changing it means editing one number.

animation-loop.stem: Where must blocks go to be repeated?
options: Inside the C-shaped mouth of the loop
animation-loop.why: Only blocks inside the loop's mouth are repeated.

animation-loop.stem: What is one pass through a loop called?
animation-loop.why: Each time round the loop is one iteration.

animation-loop.stem: 'repeat 4 [move 100 steps, turn 90 degrees]' draws what path?
animation-loop.why: Four moves with four 90-degree turns traces a square.

animation-loop.stem: You want a walking animation to go on longer. What do you change?
animation-loop.why: The repeat count controls how many times the animation cycles.

animation-loop.stem: Blocks placed UNDER a repeat loop run when?
options: After the loop has finished all its repeats
At the same time as the loop
animation-loop.why: The script continues below the loop only once the loop is done.

animation-loop.stem: Which is the clearest sign you should use a loop?
options: You are about to copy the same blocks again and again
animation-loop.why: Repetition in your code is the signal to reach for a loop.

animation-loop.stem: A loop inside another loop is called:
animation-loop.why: Loops inside loops are nested — the inner one runs fully each time the outer repeats.

animation-loop.stem: 'repeat 3' containing 'repeat 4' runs the innermost blocks how many times?
animation-loop.why: 3 x 4 = 12 — the inner loop runs fully on each of the outer loop's 3 passes.

forever.stem: When should you use a forever loop instead of repeat?
options: For behaviour that should always be running
When you know the exact number of repeats
forever.why: Forever suits continuous behaviour like checking, patrolling or animating.

forever.stem: What happens to blocks placed UNDER a forever loop?
options: They run once at the end
forever.why: A forever loop never finishes, so nothing below it is ever reached.

forever.stem: How do you stop a forever loop?
options: Press the red stop sign or use 'stop all'
forever.why: Forever never ends by itself — it needs stopping.

forever.stem: Which behaviour is best in a forever loop?
options: Constantly checking if the player pressed a key
Saying hello once at the start
forever.why: Checking must repeat constantly, so it belongs in a forever loop.

forever.stem: Can two sprites each run their own forever loop at the same time?
options: No, only one at a time
forever.why: Scratch runs many scripts at once, which is how games feel alive.

forever.stem: You put 'set score to 0' inside a forever loop. What goes wrong?
options: The score resets constantly and never goes up
forever.why: Resetting inside the loop wipes the score every frame — it belongs at the start.

forever.stem: Which is the better structure for a game?
options: Several small scripts, each with one job
One giant forever loop containing everything
forever.why: Separate scripts for separate behaviours are far easier to read and debug.

forever.stem: A patrolling enemy that moves back and forth all game should use:
forever.why: Patrolling should continue for the whole game, so forever fits.

forever.stem: What is the difference between 'repeat 10' and 'forever'?
options: Repeat runs a set number of times, forever never stops
forever.why: The key difference is whether the number of repeats is known.

forever.stem: Your project cannot be stopped by the red sign. What is most likely?
options: A script is stuck in a loop with no screen refresh
forever.why: Tight loops can block stopping — adding a small wait inside usually helps.

options: Something that happens and starts a script
events-key.why: Events are triggers — a key press, a click, the green flag.

events-key.stem: How many scripts do you need for four arrow keys?
events-key.why: Each key press event needs its own hat block and script.

events-key.stem: Which block moves a sprite left?
events-key.why: Negative x moves left; positive x moves right.

options: The rounded block on top that listens for an event
The last block in a script
events-key.why: Hat blocks sit on top and start the script when their event happens.

events-key.stem: Which block moves a sprite up?
You press a key and nothing happens. What is worth checking first?
options: That you clicked the stage so it has focus
That the sprite is big enough
events-key.why: Scratch needs the stage focused to receive key presses.

events-key.stem: Which trigger suits a character that reacts when tapped?
events-key.why: 'when this sprite clicked' fires when the player clicks that sprite.

events-key.stem: What makes an event-driven program different from a straight sequence?
options: Scripts wait for something to happen before running
events-key.why: Event-driven code responds to triggers rather than running straight through.

events-key.stem: Only one arrow key works in your game. What is the likely cause?
options: The other keys have no scripts of their own
events-key.why: Each key needs its own hat block; one script cannot cover them all.

events-key.stem: Which key event would make a sprite jump?
options: when I start as a clone
events-key.why: Space is the usual jump key, triggered by a key-press event.

events-click.stem: Where must you click to test 'when this sprite clicked'?
options: On the sprite on the stage
On the sprite in the sprite list
events-click.why: Clicking the thumbnail in the sprite list only selects it — you must click it on the stage.

events-click.stem: Which trigger starts the whole project?
events-click.why: The green flag is the standard project start.

events-click.stem: Your click reaction is too fast to notice. What helps?
options: Add a wait or a longer effect
events-click.why: Reactions need enough time on screen for the player to see them.

options: It responds to what the player does
It runs for a long time
events-click.why: Interactivity means the program reacts to the player's input.

events-click.stem: Three sprites should each do something different when clicked. What do you need?
options: A separate click script on each sprite
events-click.why: Each sprite carries its own click script and its own reaction.

events-click.stem: Which trigger fires when the scene changes?
events-click.why: It lets sprites react to a change of scene.

events-click.stem: Why give a click a sound as well as a visual change?
options: Feedback makes the interaction feel satisfying
events-click.why: Multiple kinds of feedback make an action feel responsive and clear.

events-click.stem: Which is the best trigger for a start button on a title screen?
options: when I start as a clone
events-click.why: The player clicks the button, so a click event is right.

events-click.stem: You coded a click reaction but on the wrong sprite. What do you check?
options: Which sprite was selected when you added the code
events-click.why: Code always belongs to the selected sprite.

options: The thing that starts a script running
The last block in a script
events-click.why: A trigger is the event that causes the script to run.

coordinates.why: 0,0 is the middle of the Scratch stage.
In Scratch, larger y values are higher up the stage.

coordinates.stem: What is the difference between 'set x to 10' and 'change x by 10'?
options: Set jumps to 10; change moves 10 further
coordinates.why: Set gives an exact position; change adjusts relative to where the sprite already is.

coordinates.stem: What is the usual range of x on the stage?
coordinates.why: The stage is 480 wide, so x runs roughly -240 to 240.

coordinates.stem: What is the usual range of y?
coordinates.why: The stage is 360 tall, so y runs roughly -180 to 180.

coordinates.stem: Your sprite keeps disappearing off the edge. What is likely wrong?
options: The coordinate values are outside the stage range
coordinates.why: Values beyond the stage bounds put the sprite out of view.

coordinates.stem: Which block sends a sprite to an exact place instantly?
coordinates.why: 'go to' is an instant jump to exact coordinates.

coordinates.stem: Which block reports how far right a sprite is?
coordinates.why: The x position block reports the sprite's left-right coordinate.

coordinates.stem: To move a sprite to the top right corner you would use roughly:
coordinates.why: Positive x is right and positive y is up, so both should be positive.

coordinates.stem: Why is x, y like Battleships?
options: Both use two numbers to find an exact spot on a grid
coordinates.why: Coordinates are grid references — the same idea as a Battleships square.

glide.stem: What does the seconds number in a glide block control?
glide.why: It sets the duration, which controls how fast the journey looks.

glide.stem: When would you choose glide over 'go to'?
options: When the movement should be seen, not instant
glide.why: Glide shows the journey; go to is an instant jump.

glide.stem: Your glide looks jumpy. What usually helps?
options: Use a longer duration such as 1 second
glide.why: Very short glides look like teleports; longer ones read as smooth travel.

glide.stem: Which block makes a sprite face the direction it is travelling?
glide.why: Pointing towards the target makes the movement look natural.

glide.stem: A glide of 0.2 seconds compared with 3 seconds feels:
glide.why: Shorter duration over the same distance means faster movement.

glide.stem: Which is best for a rocket flying slowly across space?
glide.why: A long glide shows a slow, visible journey.

glide.stem: Why might you combine glide with 'point towards'?
options: So the sprite faces where it is going
glide.why: Facing the direction of travel makes movement believable.

glide.stem: Your sprite arrives sideways after gliding. What fixes it?
options: Set the rotation style or point in direction 90
glide.why: Rotation style controls how the sprite is allowed to turn.

options: An exact x and y position over time
glide.why: Glide targets exact coordinates, just spread over a duration.
Glide interpolates the movement, which is what makes it look smooth.

backdrops.stem: Where does backdrop code usually live?
backdrops.why: The Stage has its own code area for backdrop behaviour.

backdrops.stem: How can a sprite react when the scene changes?
backdrops.why: That hat block lets scenery drive character behaviour.

backdrops.stem: How do you stop a sprite appearing in the wrong scene?
options: Use hide and show with the backdrop change
backdrops.why: Hiding and showing per scene is the reliable way to manage visibility.

options: The picture behind everything on the stage
backdrops.why: The backdrop is the stage's background image.

backdrops.stem: Which block moves to the next background?
backdrops.why: 'next backdrop' steps through the backdrop list.

backdrops.stem: Why add a wait after switching backdrops in a story?
options: So the player has time to see the new scene
backdrops.why: Instant changes give the player no time to read or absorb the scene.

backdrops.stem: In a film, how do you know the location changed?
backdrops.why: Changing the background is exactly what a backdrop switch does.

backdrops.stem: You added backdrop code to a sprite by mistake. What should you do?
backdrops.why: Backdrop logic belongs on the Stage.

backdrops.stem: Which is a good use of multiple backdrops?
options: Showing different scenes in a story
backdrops.why: Multiple backdrops let you build scenes and settings.

backdrops.stem: A title screen and a game screen are best built with:
options: Two backdrops plus show/hide on sprites
backdrops.why: Separate backdrops with managed sprite visibility create clean screens.

size-effects.stem: Why should you set size at the start of a project?
options: So it resets to the same size every run
size-effects.why: Without a reset, size changes carry over into the next game.

size-effects.stem: What does the ghost effect do?
size-effects.why: Ghost controls transparency — 100 is fully invisible.

size-effects.stem: How do you make a collected item disappear?
size-effects.why: Hiding removes it from view when it is picked up.

size-effects.stem: Your sprite is invisible when the game starts. What is the likely cause?
options: It was hidden last game and never shown
size-effects.why: A hidden sprite stays hidden until a 'show' block runs.

size-effects.stem: Your sprite grows bigger every time you play. What fixes it?
options: Use 'set size to 100' at the start
Use 'change size by' at the start
size-effects.why: 'Set' forces an exact size; 'change' just keeps adding.

options: Makes the sprite half its normal size
size-effects.why: Size is a percentage where 100% is the sprite's normal size.

size-effects.stem: Which block removes leftover colour or ghost effects?
size-effects.why: 'clear graphic effects' resets all visual effects on a sprite.

size-effects.stem: Which combination makes a satisfying 'collect' animation?
options: Grow, fade with ghost, then hide
size-effects.why: Layering a grow, a fade and a hide gives clear, pleasing feedback.

size-effects.stem: What three things should most projects reset at the start?
size-effects.why: Resetting position, size and show/hide prevents a whole class of bugs.

size-effects.stem: A ghost effect of 100 means the sprite is:
size-effects.why: Ghost 100 is fully transparent; 0 is fully solid.

sound-play.stem: What is the difference between 'start sound' and 'play sound until done'?
options: Start carries straight on; until done waits for the sound to finish
sound-play.why: It matters when the next block should run.

sound-play.stem: Where do a sprite's sounds live?
sound-play.why: Each sprite has its own Sounds tab.

sound-play.stem: Your sounds overlap into noise. What helps?
options: Use 'play until done' or stop other sounds
sound-play.why: Overlapping starts pile sounds on top of each other.

sound-play.stem: Why does sound matter in a game?
options: It gives feedback and makes actions feel real
It makes the game run faster
sound-play.why: Sound is cheap polish that communicates what just happened.

sound-play.stem: Which block would you use for a jump sound that should not pause the game?
sound-play.why: Start sound lets the action continue immediately.
'stop all sounds' silences audio without stopping the project.

sound-play.stem: You hear nothing at all. What should you check?
options: The sprite has the sound and the volume is up
sound-play.why: Check the sound is attached to the sprite and the system volume is on.

sound-play.stem: Which block makes the sound quieter?
sound-play.why: A negative change reduces the volume.

sound-play.stem: When should you use 'play sound until done'?
options: When the next action must wait for the sound
sound-play.why: It is right when timing depends on the sound finishing.

sound-play.stem: A good rule for game sounds is:
options: Every important player action gets its own sound
sound-play.why: Distinct sounds tell the player exactly what happened.

options: Pauses that script for one second
wait-timing.why: It pauses only the script it is in; other scripts keep running.

wait-timing.stem: Which wait is better for smooth animation?
wait-timing.why: Short waits give smooth motion; long ones look like slideshow steps.

wait-timing.stem: Everything seems to happen at once. What is missing?
wait-timing.why: Without waits the steps run too fast to distinguish.

wait-timing.stem: How do two sprites take turns speaking?
options: Match one sprite's wait to the other's speaking time
wait-timing.why: Timing their waits to each other keeps a conversation in order.

options: Pauses until a condition becomes true
Waits a fixed number of seconds
wait-timing.why: It waits on a condition rather than a fixed time.

wait-timing.stem: Your animation is jerky. What should you try?
wait-timing.why: Shorter waits mean more frames per second, which looks smoother.

wait-timing.stem: Why can timing with waits drift out of sync over a long project?
options: Small differences add up over time
wait-timing.why: This is exactly why broadcasts are better for coordinating sprites later on.

wait-timing.stem: A sprite should pause until the player presses space. Best block?
wait-timing.why: Wait until responds to the player rather than guessing a time.

wait-timing.stem: In a 3-step scene, waits let you control:
options: The order and pacing of the steps
wait-timing.why: Waits are how you choreograph when each thing happens.

options: They pause only the script they are inside
wait-timing.why: Other scripts continue running during a wait.

if-basic.stem: What shape of block fits in an 'if' condition slot?
if-basic.why: Boolean blocks are pointy and report true or false.

if-basic.stem: Why is an 'if' usually placed inside a forever loop?
options: So it keeps checking again and again
if-basic.why: Checked once, an if only tests at that instant; games need constant checking.

options: Something that is either true or false
if-basic.why: Conditions are true/false tests that decide whether code runs.

if-basic.stem: 'IF it rains THEN take an umbrella' is an example of:
if-basic.why: It runs an action only when a condition is true.

if-basic.stem: Your if block never seems to do anything. What is a likely cause?
options: It is not inside a loop, so it checked only once
if-basic.why: A one-time check usually misses the moment the condition becomes true.

options: A value that is either true or false
if-basic.why: Booleans are the true/false values that conditions produce.

if-basic.stem: Which block reports whether a sprite is touching another?
if-basic.why: It is a boolean sensing block that reports true or false.

if-basic.stem: An empty condition slot in an if block means:
options: The if will not do anything useful
if-basic.why: Without a condition there is nothing to test.

if-basic.stem: What is the difference between 'if' and 'wait until'?
options: If checks once and moves on; wait until pauses until true
if-basic.why: One tests and continues, the other blocks the script until true.

if-basic.stem: Which structure detects a collision continuously?
if-basic.why: Continuous detection needs the check repeated inside a forever loop.

sensing-touch.stem: How does a game know two things collided?
sensing-touch.why: Sensing blocks detect when sprites touch.

options: The colour picked is not an exact match
sensing-touch.why: Colour sensing needs the exact shade — use the eyedropper on the real pixel.

sensing-touch.stem: A collision fires many times per second. How do you make it happen once?
options: Hide the object or add a short wait
sensing-touch.why: Removing the object or pausing stops repeated triggering.

sensing-touch.stem: Sprites look like they touch but nothing happens. What is a likely reason?
sensing-touch.why: Scratch senses the visible pixels, and costumes often have invisible padding.

sensing-touch.stem: Which block detects touching a coloured line, such as a race track?
sensing-touch.why: Colour sensing is ideal for tracks, walls and platforms.

options: How far away another sprite or the mouse is
sensing-touch.why: Useful for 'the enemy notices you when you get close'.

sensing-touch.stem: In a collect game, what should happen when the player touches a coin?
options: Score up, sound, and the coin hides
sensing-touch.why: Collision is a trigger for feedback and game logic.

sensing-touch.stem: Where should a touching check normally live?
sensing-touch.why: Detection must repeat constantly, so it goes inside forever.

sensing-touch.stem: Which is a boolean sensing block?
sensing-touch.why: It is pointy and reports true or false.

sensing-touch.stem: Why keep all your platforms exactly the same colour?
options: So one colour check works for all of them
sensing-touch.why: A single consistent colour makes collision detection reliable.

sensing-key.stem: Why is 'key pressed?' sensing smoother than key-press events?
options: It checks constantly with no key-repeat delay
sensing-key.why: Polling avoids the pause before a held key starts repeating.

sensing-key.stem: How do you allow diagonal movement?
options: Put all the ifs in the same forever loop
sensing-key.why: In one loop, two conditions can both be true on the same pass.
Polling is repeatedly asking 'is this true yet?'.

sensing-key.stem: Your sprite moves far too fast. What do you change?
options: Use a smaller change value like 3
sensing-key.why: The change amount per frame controls speed.

sensing-key.stem: Old key-event scripts still exist alongside new sensing scripts. What happens?
options: They fight each other and movement feels odd
sensing-key.why: Two systems moving the same sprite cause conflicts — delete the old one.

sensing-key.stem: Which block reports true while a key is held down?
sensing-key.why: It is a boolean that stays true for as long as the key is down.

sensing-key.stem: Which structure gives responsive four-way control?
options: forever with four if blocks inside
sensing-key.why: One loop polling four keys is the standard responsive control pattern.

sensing-key.stem: Games usually prefer polling over events for movement because:
options: It feels smoother and allows diagonals
sensing-key.why: Smoothness and simultaneous keys are why games poll.

sensing-key.stem: What is the trade-off with key events?
options: Simple to build but movement stutters
sensing-key.why: Events are simpler but have the key-repeat delay.

sensing-key.stem: How would you add a 'run faster while shift is held'?
options: Nest another if checking the shift key

random.stem: Why use random numbers in a game?
options: Every play is different, so it stays interesting
random.why: Unpredictability is what makes a game worth replaying.

random.stem: Which range keeps a sprite on stage horizontally?
random.why: The stage is about -240 to 240 wide, so -200 to 200 is safely inside.

random.stem: Your sprite is vibrating in place. What is the likely cause?
options: A random position is being picked every frame
random.why: Re-picking a random value constantly makes the sprite jitter.

random.stem: Which block gives a different number each time?
random.why: Pick random returns a new value on each use.

random.stem: How can random make timing feel natural?
random.why: Varying the gaps stops events feeling mechanical.
It gives a whole number from 1 to 6, exactly like a dice.

random.stem: Where should you pick a random value if the sprite should keep it for a while?
options: Once, before the loop or after a wait
random.why: Picking once and keeping it avoids constant re-rolling.

random.stem: Which makes a target appear unpredictably?
options: go to x: (pick random -200 to 200) y: (pick random -150 to 150)
random.why: Random coordinates place the target somewhere new each time.

random.stem: A range that keeps a sprite fully on stage vertically is about:
random.why: The stage is roughly -180 to 180 tall, so -150 to 150 stays safely inside.

random.stem: Combining random size, position and wait creates:
random.why: Layering randomness makes a scene feel alive rather than repetitive.

options: A named box that stores a value you can change
variable-score.why: Think of it as a labelled box holding one value.

variable-score.stem: What is the difference between 'set' and 'change by'?
options: Set puts an exact value in; change adds to what is there
variable-score.why: Set replaces the value; change adjusts it.

variable-score.stem: Why 'set score to 0' when the flag is clicked?
variable-score.why: Without a reset the previous game's score carries over.

variable-score.stem: Your score jumps up by many points at once. What is the cause?
options: The change block is running every frame in a loop
variable-score.why: The collision fires repeatedly — hide the item or add a wait.

variable-score.stem: What makes a good variable name?
variable-score.why: Clear names make code readable — a real programming habit.
Change adds to the current value.

variable-score.stem: How do you let the player see their score?
options: Show the variable on the stage
variable-score.why: Players need to see the score for it to matter.

variable-score.stem: A high-score variable should update when:
options: The new score beats the old high score
variable-score.why: That comparison is what makes it a high score.

variable-score.stem: Which variable option gives every clone its own copy?
variable-score.why: 'For this sprite only' creates a local copy per sprite and per clone.

variable-score.stem: What is stored in a variable?
variable-score.why: One variable holds one value; lists hold many.

options: When there are exactly two possible outcomes

if-else.stem: If the condition is false, which part runs?
if-else.why: Else is the path taken when the condition is false.

if-else.stem: Can both branches of an if-else run at the same time?
if-else.why: Exactly one branch runs each time.

if-else.stem: Both your win and lose messages appear. What went wrong?
options: You used two separate ifs, or the conditions overlap
if-else.why: If-else guarantees only one path runs.

if-else.stem: 'If you finish your homework, then you play, ELSE you keep working' is:
if-else.why: Two outcomes, chosen by one condition.

if-else.stem: Your else branch never runs. What should you check?
options: Whether the condition is always true
if-else.why: If the condition can never be false, else is unreachable.

if-else.stem: How would you handle three outcomes such as win, draw and lose?
options: Nest an if inside the else
if-else.why: Nesting conditionals handles more than two cases.

if-else.stem: A quiz answer check is best written as:
if-else.why: There are exactly two outcomes, which is what if-else is for.

options: Following which branch runs, step by step
if-else.why: Tracing is a core debugging skill.

if-else.stem: Which is tidier than two ifs with opposite conditions?
if-else.why: If-else expresses the either/or clearly and cannot double-fire.

repeat-until.stem: Which loop suits 'keep going until you reach the goal'?
repeat-until.why: Repeat until runs while working towards a condition.

repeat-until.stem: Why might a repeat-until loop never stop?
options: The condition can never become true
repeat-until.why: If nothing can make the condition true, the loop runs forever.

options: Pauses the script until a condition is true
repeat-until.why: It is the pausing version of the same idea.

options: The condition was already true at the start
repeat-until.why: If it is true before the loop begins, the loop body never runs.

repeat-until.stem: 'Keep stirring until it is smooth' is like which loop?
repeat-until.why: The end is defined by a condition, not a count.

repeat-until.stem: Which loop should you use when you know the exact number of repeats?
repeat-until.why: A fixed count means a plain repeat loop.

repeat-until.stem: Which loop never ends on its own?
repeat-until.why: Forever continues until the project is stopped.

repeat-until.stem: How would you end a loop on two possible conditions?
repeat-until.why: Combining conditions with 'or' ends the loop when either happens.

repeat-until.stem: A chasing sprite should move until it catches the target. Best structure?
repeat-until.why: The chase should end exactly when it catches the target.
It ends only the script it is in, leaving others running.

mouse-follow.stem: How do you make a sprite face the mouse?
mouse-follow.why: Point towards rotates the sprite to face the target.

mouse-follow.stem: How do you build a paddle that slides side to side only?
mouse-follow.why: Setting only x keeps the paddle on a fixed height.

mouse-follow.stem: Following code must sit inside which block?
mouse-follow.why: Following must be continuous, so it goes in a forever loop.

mouse-follow.stem: Your sprite sits exactly on the pointer and hides it. What helps?
options: Offset it, for example change y by -20
mouse-follow.why: An offset keeps the cursor visible.

mouse-follow.stem: Your following sprite spins wildly. What fixes it?
mouse-follow.why: Rotation style controls whether it flips or spins fully.

mouse-follow.stem: Which blocks report where the mouse is?
How could a sprite follow only when the mouse is close?
mouse-follow.why: Adding a distance condition makes the following conditional.
It matches the pointer's position exactly.

mouse-follow.stem: For eyes that track the player, the best block is:
mouse-follow.why: Pointing rotates the eyes to look at the cursor without moving them.

mouse-follow.stem: In a Pong-style game, the paddle usually follows:
mouse-follow.why: Constraining to one axis keeps the paddle on its side of the court.

bounce.stem: Which block keeps a sprite on the stage by reversing it at the edge?
bounce.why: It flips the sprite's direction when it reaches the edge.

bounce.stem: Your bouncing sprite is upside-down. What fixes it?
bounce.why: The default all-around rotation lets sprites flip over.

bounce.stem: Where must the bounce block go?
options: Inside the forever loop with the move block
bounce.why: It must run every frame alongside the movement.

bounce.stem: How do you make each run take a different path?
options: point in direction (pick random 1 to 360) at the start
bounce.why: A random starting direction makes each run unique.

bounce.stem: Your sprite gets stuck vibrating on the edge. What helps?
options: Move it inward slightly or increase the step size
bounce.why: It is re-triggering the bounce every frame while still on the edge.

bounce.stem: A patrolling enemy is usually built from:
options: move plus if on edge bounce inside forever
bounce.why: That pairing creates continuous back-and-forth movement.

bounce.stem: What real-world idea does bouncing model?
options: A ball rebounding off a wall
bounce.why: The direction reverses on impact, just like a rebound.
It keeps characters the right way up while still facing left or right.

bounce.stem: Two bouncing sprites should react when they hit each other. What do you add?
The bounce block works on which boundary?
bounce.why: It specifically handles the stage edge.

options: A mistake that makes a program behave wrongly
debug-basics.why: A bug is an error in the code causing unexpected behaviour.

debug-basics.stem: What is the first step when debugging?
options: Say what it should do versus what it actually does
debug-basics.why: Naming the gap between expected and actual focuses the search.

debug-basics.stem: Why change only one thing at a time?
options: So you know which change fixed it
debug-basics.why: Changing many things at once hides which one mattered.

debug-basics.stem: How can you test one script on its own?
options: Click just that stack of blocks
debug-basics.why: Clicking a stack runs it in isolation.

debug-basics.stem: How can a 'say' block help you debug?
options: It shows you what the code thinks is happening
debug-basics.why: Displaying a value reveals what is really going on inside the code.

debug-basics.stem: Your project runs too fast to see the problem. What helps?
options: Add waits to slow it down
debug-basics.why: Slowing execution makes the failure visible.

debug-basics.stem: After fixing a bug you should:
options: Run it again to confirm the fix
debug-basics.why: Fixing without re-testing is how bugs come back.

debug-basics.stem: If the program does something strange, who is usually right?
options: The computer — it does exactly what it was told
debug-basics.why: The computer follows instructions literally; find what it was actually told.

debug-basics.stem: Why is debugging a normal part of programming?
options: All programmers spend much of their time finding bugs
debug-basics.why: Debugging is the job, not a sign of failure.

debug-basics.stem: A good habit before making big changes is:
options: Keep a copy so you can go back
debug-basics.why: A safe copy lets you experiment without losing working code.

options: The rule that decides the player has won
game-win-lose.why: It is the test that ends the game in success.

game-win-lose.stem: Why use '>' rather than '=' when checking a score?
options: The score might skip past the exact number
game-win-lose.why: If the score jumps by 2 or 5, an exact match can be missed entirely.

game-win-lose.stem: Your win message flashes and disappears instantly. What is wrong?
options: 'stop all' ran before the message could be read
game-win-lose.why: Say the message first, give it time, then stop.

game-win-lose.stem: Your game ends the moment it starts. What is the likely cause?
options: Variables were not reset, so the condition was already true
game-win-lose.why: Resetting score and lives at the start prevents this.

game-win-lose.stem: How should the game tell the player they won?
options: A message and a backdrop change
game-win-lose.why: Clear feedback is essential — a silent ending confuses players.

options: The rule that ends the game in failure
game-win-lose.why: For example, lives reaching zero or time running out.

game-win-lose.stem: Why write your rules in plain English before coding?
options: It makes turning them into blocks much easier
game-win-lose.why: Designing before coding is what separates a planned game from a mess.

options: Whether the game is playing, won or lost
game-win-lose.why: Game state describes which part of the game is currently active.

game-win-lose.stem: You should test a game's endings by:
options: Deliberately triggering both win and lose
game-win-lose.why: Both endings need testing on purpose, since they are easy to get wrong.

game-win-lose.stem: Which block ends the whole project?
game-win-lose.why: 'stop all' halts every script in the project.

l1-capstone.stem: What should you do before building a big project?
options: Plan it — goal, controls, rules, win and lose
l1-capstone.why: Ten minutes of planning saves thirty minutes of confusion.

l1-capstone.stem: What should you build and test first?
l1-capstone.why: Get the core interaction working before layering features on it.

l1-capstone.stem: Why test after each layer instead of at the end?
options: It is much easier to find what broke
l1-capstone.why: Testing in layers isolates problems to the thing you just added.

l1-capstone.stem: Your project idea is far too big. What is the best response?
options: Cut it down to one screen and one mechanic
l1-capstone.why: A finished small game beats an unfinished ambitious one.

l1-capstone.stem: Which blocks should run at the start of your game?
options: Reset score, position, size and show
l1-capstone.why: Resetting state at the start prevents a whole class of bugs.

options: A project that brings together everything you have learned
l1-capstone.why: It is where all the separate skills combine into one build.

options: Demonstrating it and explaining your code choices
l1-capstone.why: Explaining your decisions shows real understanding.

options: Improving a project through repeated testing
l1-capstone.why: Iteration means build, test, improve, repeat.

l1-capstone.stem: A good order for building a game is:
l1-capstone.why: Build the core first, then layer features, testing at each stage.

l1-capstone.stem: Why write instructions for your player?
options: They cannot see your code or read your mind
l1-capstone.why: A game that needs explaining in person is not finished.

operators-math.stem: Where do green operator blocks go?
operators-math.why: Operators are values, so they slot inside other blocks.
10 mod 3 is 1, because 3 goes into 10 three times with 1 left over.

operators-math.stem: How would you double a score?
Your division shows a long decimal. What tidies it?
operators-math.why: Round gives the nearest whole number.

operators-math.stem: 'set score to ((score) + (5))' does the same as:
operators-math.why: Both add 5 to the current score.

operators-math.stem: How could you detect every 5th point?
operators-math.why: Mod 5 equals 0 at 5, 10, 15 and so on.

operators-math.stem: 7 coins worth 10 points each. Which expression gives the score?
operators-math.why: Multiplication is repeated addition — 7 lots of 10.

options: Blocks combined to work out a value
operators-math.why: An expression calculates and reports a value.

operators-math.stem: Your nested expression is impossible to read. What helps?
options: Build it in stages using a helper variable
operators-math.why: Breaking a calculation into named steps makes it readable.
The minus operator subtracts the second value from the first.

operators-compare.why: Comparisons are booleans — they report true or false.

operators-compare.stem: Why is '>' safer than '=' for a score check?
options: The score might skip the exact value
operators-compare.why: If the score jumps by 2, it can step straight over the exact number.
Greater than 9 includes 10 and everything above.

operators-compare.stem: You put a comparison into a 'say' block and clicked it. What appears?
operators-compare.why: Seeing the boolean directly makes the idea concrete.

operators-compare.stem: Which block checks if lives have run out?
operators-compare.why: Less than 1 catches 0 and any negative value.

operators-compare.stem: Your comparison compares text instead of numbers. What should you check?
options: That the variable holds a number
operators-compare.why: A variable holding text will not compare numerically as expected.

operators-compare.stem: Comparison blocks are used most often inside:
Which reports true when the first value is smaller?
For a grade band 'over 90 is excellent', you would use:
operators-compare.why: Greater than 90 defines the top band.
Pointy blocks report true or false and fit condition slots.

operators-logic.why: Or needs just one condition to hold.

options: Flips true to false and false to true

operators-logic.stem: 'You may have ice cream if you finish dinner AND it is not a school night' uses:
operators-logic.why: It combines two conditions with and, one of them negated.

operators-logic.stem: Which condition means 'hit by either hazard'?
operators-logic.why: Either hazard should count, so use or.

operators-logic.stem: 'Keep moving while not touching a wall' uses which structure?
options: repeat until, or not with a condition
operators-logic.why: Not inverts the touching test so movement continues while free.

operators-logic.stem: Your combined condition behaves oddly. What is a good first step?
operators-logic.why: Isolating each part shows which one misbehaves.

operators-logic.stem: How many rows does a truth table for two conditions have?
operators-logic.why: Each condition can be true or false: 2 x 2 = 4 combinations.

operators-logic.stem: To win you must reach the goal AND collect all items. Which block?
A very complex condition is easier to manage if you:
options: Store part of it in a variable such as 'ready'
operators-logic.why: Naming part of the logic makes it readable and testable.

options: change the variable by -1 with a wait
variable-timer.why: Negative change plus a wait produces a countdown.

variable-timer.stem: Your countdown races to zero instantly. What is missing?
variable-timer.why: Without a wait, the loop runs many times per second.

options: Sets the built-in timer back to zero
variable-timer.why: Reset it at the start so timing is fair.

variable-timer.stem: Why do timers make games more exciting?
variable-timer.why: Time pressure changes how a game feels to play.

options: set time to 30, repeat until time = 0 [wait 1, change time by -1]
variable-timer.why: Set, then decrease once per second until zero.

variable-timer.stem: Your timer keeps running after the game ends. What fixes it?
options: Use 'stop all' or a game-state check
variable-timer.why: The timer loop needs stopping when the game ends.

options: Seconds since it was last reset

variable-timer.stem: A timer that counts up instead of down means you used:
variable-timer.why: The sign of the change controls direction.

variable-timer.stem: How could a bonus give extra time?
variable-timer.why: Change adds to the remaining time.

variable-timer.stem: Making the timer flash under 5 seconds is an example of:
variable-timer.why: Visual urgency communicates the state of play.

variable-lives.stem: Why do games give three lives rather than one?
options: Instant failure feels unfair and discouraging
variable-lives.why: Fairness is a deliberate design decision.

variable-lives.stem: One touch drains all three lives instantly. What is the fix?
options: Add a brief wait or move the player away after a hit
variable-lives.why: The collision is firing every frame — pause or separate them.

variable-lives.stem: Which block takes a life away?
variable-lives.why: A negative change reduces the value.

variable-lives.stem: What should happen when lives reach zero?
options: The game ends with a clear message
variable-lives.why: Zero lives is the lose condition and needs feedback.

options: Returning the player to a safe start position
variable-lives.why: Respawning puts the player back into play after a hit.

variable-lives.stem: Lives carry over between games. What is missing?
variable-lives.why: Variables must be reset when the game begins.

variable-lives.stem: Which check is safest for game over?
variable-lives.why: Less than 1 also catches negative values if lives overshoot.

variable-lives.stem: How could you show health without a number?
options: Use costumes or sprite size as a health bar
variable-lives.why: Visual health is easier for young players to read at a glance.

variable-lives.stem: A pick-up that restores health would use:
options: change health by a positive number

variable-lives.stem: Brief invincibility after a hit is used because:
options: It stops one collision draining every life
variable-lives.why: It is the standard fix for repeated-collision damage.

options: Sends a message every sprite can hear

broadcast.stem: What is the difference from 'broadcast and wait'?
options: And-wait pauses until all receivers finish
And-wait only works on the Stage
broadcast.why: Use and-wait when the next step depends on receivers completing.

broadcast.stem: Nothing reacts to your broadcast. What should you check?
options: The receiver is listening for the same message name

broadcast.stem: Why are broadcasts better than waits for coordinating sprites?
What is a good message name?
broadcast.why: Descriptive names keep bigger projects readable.

broadcast.stem: A referee's whistle starting eight runners is like:
broadcast.why: One signal, everyone reacts — exactly a broadcast.

broadcast.stem: Broadcasting inside a forever loop causes:
broadcast.why: Guard it or move it out, or receivers restart constantly.

broadcast.stem: Which hat block reacts to a message?
broadcast.why: It runs when that message is broadcast.

options: Sprites cooperate without being directly connected
broadcast.why: Each sprite just listens for messages it cares about.
Chains let you sequence complex behaviour across sprites.

broadcast-scenes.stem: What are the three usual game states?
options: Start, middle, end of a sprite
broadcast-scenes.why: Most games move between these three screens.

broadcast-scenes.stem: How do you move between game states?
broadcast-scenes.why: Messages signal a state change to every sprite.

broadcast-scenes.stem: What must happen when a new game starts?
broadcast-scenes.why: Without a reset the new game inherits the old game's state.

broadcast-scenes.stem: Menu sprites are still visible during play. What is missing?
options: A 'hide' on each when the game starts
broadcast-scenes.why: Every sprite must decide what to show or hide per state.

broadcast-scenes.stem: A start button on a title screen should:
broadcast-scenes.why: The click triggers the state change.

options: A design that moves between defined states on events
broadcast-scenes.why: Boxes and arrows: states and the events that move between them.

broadcast-scenes.stem: Two states seem to run at once. What is the likely cause?
options: The old state's loops were never stopped
broadcast-scenes.why: Stop the previous state's scripts or guard them with a state variable.

broadcast-scenes.stem: Why is a title screen worth adding?
options: It tells the player what to do before they start
broadcast-scenes.why: It sets expectations and makes a project feel finished.

broadcast-scenes.stem: Restarting your game leaves the old score. What fixes it?
broadcast-scenes.why: Every restart must clear game state.

options: A way to stop game loops and resume them
broadcast-scenes.why: Pausing means suspending the playing state cleanly.

options: A copy of a sprite made while the project runs
clones-basic.why: Clones let one sprite become many at runtime.

clones-basic.stem: Which block runs for each new clone?
options: when I start as a clone
clones-basic.why: Each clone runs that script separately.

options: They pile up and slow the project down
clones-basic.why: Undeleted clones accumulate and destroy performance.

clones-basic.stem: Your clones never appear. What is a common cause?
options: The original is not hidden or the clones never show
clones-basic.why: Usually the original should hide and each clone should show.

clones-basic.stem: All your clones move identically and overlap. What helps?
options: Give each a random position or wait when it starts
clones-basic.why: Randomising per clone makes them behave individually.

clones-basic.stem: A game with 50 falling asteroids is best built with:
Which block makes a copy at runtime?

options: forever [create clone of myself, wait 1 seconds]
clones-basic.why: A loop with a wait produces a steady stream of clones.

clones-basic.stem: Each clone has its own copy of which variables?
clones-basic.why: Local variables are per-sprite and per-clone.

clones-basic.stem: When should a falling clone be deleted?
options: When it goes off-screen or is caught
clones-basic.why: Deleting when finished keeps the clone count under control.

clones-advanced.stem: Why use a 'for this sprite only' variable with clones?
options: So each clone has its own value, such as speed
clones-advanced.why: Local variables give each clone individual properties.

clones-advanced.stem: How do you build a formation of clones?
What is a wave of enemies?
options: A group of clones spawned together
clones-advanced.why: Waves are a design tool for pacing difficulty.

clones-advanced.stem: Your frame rate collapses. What should you do?
options: Cap the clone count and delete off-screen clones
clones-advanced.why: Performance depends on how many clones exist at once.

clones-advanced.stem: How do you make each wave harder?
options: Increase speed or clone count each wave
clones-advanced.why: Escalating difficulty keeps the player engaged.

clones-advanced.stem: All clones unexpectedly share one value. What went wrong?
options: The variable was made 'for all sprites'
clones-advanced.why: Global variables are shared; local ones are per clone.

options: A wave of 10 clones spread over time

clones-advanced.stem: How can clones have different types, such as good and bad?
options: Use a local variable to store the type
clones-advanced.why: A per-clone variable lets one sprite behave in several ways.

clones-advanced.stem: Clones spawning on top of each other is fixed by:
options: Staggering with a wait or spreading positions
clones-advanced.why: Spacing them out in time or position separates them.

options: Each clone follows the same rule from a different start
clones-advanced.why: Identical rules with different starting values create formations.

lists.stem: What number is the first item in a Scratch list?
What is the difference between a variable and a list?
options: A variable holds one value, a list holds many

lists.stem: How do you pick a random item safely?
options: item (pick random 1 to (length of list)) of list
lists.why: The range must be 1 to the list's length.

lists.stem: Your list doubles in size every run. What is missing?
lists.why: Without clearing, items are appended again each run.

lists.stem: Which block checks whether a list holds a value?
Two parallel lists for questions and answers must:
options: Stay aligned, so item 3 matches item 3
lists.why: Their positions correspond, so alignment is essential.

lists.stem: A high-score table is best stored in:
lists.why: Lists hold multiple scores in order.

lists.stem: Which block adds an item to the end of a list?
A shopping list is a good real-world example of:
lists.why: Many items stored together under one name.

options: A block you make that runs your own script
myblocks.why: You define what it does, then use it like any other block.

options: Less repetition and much clearer code
myblocks.why: They remove duplication and give code meaningful names.

options: Hiding detail behind a simple name
myblocks.why: 'Make a cup of tea' hides twelve steps behind three words.

myblocks.stem: You made a custom block but nothing changed. What is likely?
options: You defined it but never used it in a script
myblocks.why: The definition must be called from your main script.

myblocks.stem: Which is a good custom block name?
myblocks.why: Names should say what the block does.

options: The blocks your custom block runs
myblocks.why: The define script is the block's body.

myblocks.stem: When is a custom block most clearly needed?
options: When the same blocks appear in several places
myblocks.why: Repeated code is the signal to refactor.
