options: Restructuring code to be clearer without changing what it does
myblocks.why: It improves the structure, not the behaviour.
Single-purpose blocks are readable and reusable.

myblocks.stem: After refactoring, your main script should:
options: Read like a list of clear instructions
myblocks.why: That readability is the whole point of abstraction.

options: A value you pass into your block
myblocks-params.why: Parameters make one block work for many situations.

myblocks-params.stem: Where do you use the parameter?
options: Inside the define, dragged from the hat
myblocks-params.why: Drag the orange oval from the define hat into the blocks inside.

myblocks-params.stem: Why is one block with an input better than five similar blocks?
Your block ignores the number you give it. What went wrong?
options: The parameter was not dragged into the blocks inside
myblocks-params.why: Without dragging it in, a fixed value is used instead.

myblocks-params.stem: Which is a good input name?
myblocks-params.why: Descriptive names make the block self-explaining.
The argument changes what the definition draws.

options: The actual value given when the block is used
myblocks-params.why: The parameter is the placeholder; the argument is the real value.

myblocks-params.stem: A block with two inputs might be:
Creating many nearly identical blocks instead of one with an input is:
options: A sign you should use a parameter
myblocks-params.why: Duplication is the signal to parameterise.

ask-answer.stem: Which block holds what the player typed?
ask-answer.why: The answer block stores the most recent reply.

ask-answer.stem: Why store the answer in a variable straight away?
ask-answer.why: Only the most recent answer is kept.

ask-answer.stem: Which block builds a sentence from words and an answer?
Your reply reads 'HelloSam'. What is missing?
options: A space at the end of 'Hello '
ask-answer.why: Join does not add spaces for you.

ask-answer.stem: What makes a chatbot feel alive?
options: Using the player's own words back to them
ask-answer.why: Personalised responses create the illusion of understanding.

ask-answer.stem: The correct block to ask a question is:
ask-answer.why: It shows an input box and waits for the reply.

ask-answer.stem: To remember three facts you need:
ask-answer.why: Each answer must be saved before the next ask.

options: Information the user gives the program
ask-answer.why: Input comes from the user into the program.

options: Waits for the player to type and press enter
ask-answer.why: 'Ask and wait' pauses for the reply.
Joining fixed text with a stored value personalises it.

quiz-logic.stem: How do you check an answer?
quiz-logic.why: An equality comparison drives the decision.

quiz-logic.stem: Where do you add the point for a correct answer?
options: In the 'then' branch of the if
quiz-logic.why: Points are awarded on the correct path.

quiz-logic.stem: Does Scratch's '=' care about capital letters for words?
quiz-logic.why: Text comparison ignores case, which is helpful for quizzes.

quiz-logic.stem: Your answer is always marked wrong. What should you check?
options: Extra spaces, or comparing the wrong variable
quiz-logic.why: A stray space stops the values matching.

quiz-logic.stem: Only the last question scores. What is missing?
options: Each question needs its own check
quiz-logic.why: Every question needs its own comparison and scoring.

quiz-logic.stem: How do you grade at the end?
quiz-logic.why: Comparisons turn a score into a grade band.

quiz-logic.stem: Using lists for questions lets you:
quiz-logic.why: Lists plus random selection make quizzes replayable.

options: Checking whether an answer is correct
quiz-logic.why: Validation compares input against what is expected.

quiz-logic.stem: Good feedback for a wrong answer includes:
options: Telling the player the correct answer
quiz-logic.why: Feedback that teaches is better than feedback that only judges.

quiz-logic.stem: Your quiz score is not reset between runs. What is missing?
quiz-logic.why: Score must be reset when the quiz begins.

gravity.stem: What does a velocity variable do?
options: Controls how fast and which way the sprite moves vertically
gravity.why: Velocity is added to the position each frame.

gravity.stem: What does gravity do to velocity?
options: Reduces it a little every frame
gravity.why: Constantly reducing velocity creates acceleration downwards.

options: change y by (velocity), change velocity by -1
gravity.why: Position changes by velocity; velocity changes by gravity.

gravity.stem: How do you make a sprite jump?
options: Set velocity to a positive number on the key press
gravity.why: A single upward velocity gives a natural arc as gravity takes over.

gravity.stem: Your sprite falls through the floor. What is missing?
options: A ground check that stops it
gravity.why: Without a boundary test nothing stops the fall.

gravity.stem: Your jump has no arc and looks instant. What is wrong?
options: Velocity is being set every frame instead of once
gravity.why: Set velocity once on the press, then let gravity act.

gravity.stem: How do you stop endless mid-air jumping?
options: Only allow a jump when the sprite is on the ground
gravity.why: Checking the ground state gates the jump.

gravity.stem: Dropping a pen shows that real gravity:
options: Makes things speed up as they fall
gravity.why: Acceleration is exactly what the velocity model reproduces.

gravity.stem: Changing gravity from -1 to -0.5 makes the game feel:
gravity.why: Tuning these numbers is game feel design.

options: A counter tracking how many jumps have been used
gravity.why: Counting jumps lets you allow exactly two.

platformer.stem: How does a game know you are standing on something?
options: It senses the platform below the player
platformer.why: Colour or sprite sensing below the player detects ground.

platformer.stem: Why use one colour for all platforms?
options: So a single check works everywhere

platformer.stem: Your player sinks into the ground. What is missing?
options: A push-out loop that moves them up until free
platformer.why: Resolve the overlap by stepping out of the platform.

platformer.stem: Which pattern climbs a player out of the ground?
platformer.why: Moving out one step at a time avoids teleporting.

platformer.stem: Your player sticks to walls. What helps?
options: Handle x and y collision separately
The area used to detect collisions
platformer.why: It is the region the game treats as solid.

platformer.stem: Collision is unreliable across your level. Likely cause?
platformer.why: Colour sensing needs an exact match.

options: Pushing the player out of a solid object
platformer.why: Detection finds the overlap; resolution fixes it.

platformer.stem: A one-way platform lets the player:
options: Jump up through it but land on top
platformer.why: It is a collision rule applied only when falling.

platformer.stem: Moving platforms require the player to:
options: Move along with the platform while standing on it
platformer.why: The player's position must follow the platform.

options: Makes the sprite draw as it moves
pen.why: The sprite leaves a trail while the pen is down.

pen.stem: What should every pen project start with?
pen.why: Otherwise old drawings pile up between runs.

pen.stem: How do you draw a square with a loop?
pen.why: Four equal sides with four 90-degree turns.

pen.stem: Where do you find the pen blocks?
options: Add the Pen extension from the bottom-left button
pen.why: Pen is an extension you must add.

pen.stem: Your sprite draws a stray line moving into position. What fixes it?
To draw a hexagon, the turn should be:
For any regular polygon the turn angle is:
options: 360 divided by the number of sides
pen.why: The turns must total one full rotation.

options: Clears everything drawn on the stage

pen.stem: A triangle needs a turn of:

pen-art.why: The repeats times the turn must total 360 to close the pattern.

pen-art.stem: What does the inner loop of a spirograph draw?
pen-art.why: The inner loop draws one shape; the outer rotates and repeats it.

pen-art.stem: How do you get a rainbow effect?
options: change pen color by a small amount in the outer loop
pen-art.why: Shifting the colour each repetition creates the gradient.

pen-art.stem: Your pattern does not close into a circle. What is wrong?
options: Repeats times turn does not equal 360
pen-art.why: The maths must total a full rotation.
The inner loop runs fully on each pass of the outer.

pen-art.stem: Your drawing runs off the stage. What helps?
pen-art.why: Smaller shapes keep the pattern on screen.

pen-art.stem: The colour never changes in your pattern. Likely cause?
options: The colour block is in the wrong loop
pen-art.why: It must be in the loop that repeats for each shape.
The rotations complete exactly one full turn.

pen-art.stem: Geometric art in Scratch mainly demonstrates:
options: Loops and angle maths working together
pen-art.why: It is maths made visible through code.

pen-art.stem: To make a denser pattern you would:
options: Increase repeats and decrease the turn angle
pen-art.why: More shapes at smaller angles fill the circle more densely.

options: The basic unit of musical time
music-blocks.why: Beats measure musical time, like steps measure distance.

music-blocks.stem: Which note number is middle C?
music-blocks.why: In Scratch, 60 is middle C; higher numbers are higher notes.

music-blocks.stem: How do you make two musical parts start together?
music-blocks.why: A single message keeps parts in sync.

music-blocks.stem: Your two parts drift out of time. What is the cause?
options: They were started separately with waits
music-blocks.why: Independent waits drift; broadcasts do not.

music-blocks.stem: Where do the music blocks come from?
music-blocks.why: Music is an extension you add.

music-blocks.stem: A repeating drum pattern is best built with:
music-blocks.why: Rhythms are repetition, which is exactly what loops do.

music-blocks.stem: Playing a drum 'for 0.25 beats' compared with 1 beat is:
music-blocks.why: The beat value sets the duration.

options: Three parts playing together, such as drums, bass and melody
How satisfying a game is to play
game-polish.why: Feel is the moment-to-moment satisfaction of playing.

game-polish.stem: Why should every player action have feedback?
options: It tells the player what happened

game-polish.stem: During a playtest, what should you do?
options: Watch silently and note every confusion
game-polish.why: A real player will have nobody to explain it to them.

game-polish.stem: Your game has effects on everything and feels chaotic. What is the fix?

options: Small effects that make actions feel good
game-polish.why: Juice is the layer of feedback that makes actions satisfying.

options: Fix the most common confusion first
game-polish.why: Prioritising by impact is how real teams iterate.

game-polish.stem: A satisfying collect effect might combine:
options: A sound, a quick grow and a fade
game-polish.why: Layered feedback across senses feels best.

game-polish.stem: If a playtester is confused, it usually means:
options: The game needs clearer feedback or instructions
game-polish.why: Confusion is information about your design.

game-polish.stem: Why not explain your game while someone tests it?
options: Because the game must speak for itself
It is a rule of Scratch
game-polish.why: Explaining hides exactly the problems you are looking for.
Good polish tells the player what is happening.

publish-share.stem: What three things do good instructions include?
options: The goal, the controls and how to win
publish-share.why: Players need to know what to do, how to do it and what success is.
Attribution is basic ethics in creative and technical work.

publish-share.stem: What should never go in a public project?
options: Personal details like your full name or school

publish-share.stem: How do you know if your instructions are clear?
options: Test them on someone who has never played
publish-share.why: Fresh eyes reveal assumptions you did not notice.

options: Building on someone else's shared project
publish-share.why: Remixing is encouraged in Scratch — with credit.

publish-share.stem: Instructions that assume the player already knows the game are:
publish-share.why: They must work for a complete newcomer.

publish-share.stem: Why does sharing your project matter?
options: Others can play it and give you feedback
publish-share.why: Feedback from real players is how projects improve.

publish-share.stem: Where do you write how to play in Scratch?
options: The Instructions field on the project page
publish-share.why: The project page has fields for instructions and credits.

publish-share.stem: If you used someone's sprite or sound you should:
publish-share.why: Credit whatever you did not make yourself.

options: Clear instructions, credits and no personal details
publish-share.why: Presentation is part of finishing the work.

options: A written description of what you will build
l2-capstone.why: Agreeing the spec before coding prevents drifting scope.

options: A checkpoint in a bigger build
l2-capstone.why: Milestones break a big project into testable stages.
If the core is not fun, nothing else will save it.

l2-capstone.stem: Your code has become an unreadable tangle. What should you do?
options: Refactor it into well-named custom blocks
l2-capstone.why: Refactoring restores readability without changing behaviour.

l2-capstone.stem: Your project is far too ambitious. Best response?
options: Cut to three features and finish them well
l2-capstone.why: A finished focused project beats an unfinished sprawling one.

l2-capstone.stem: When should you test during a long build?
l2-capstone.why: Testing per milestone isolates problems to recent work.

l2-capstone.stem: Which counts as a Level 2 technique?
options: Clones, broadcasts, custom blocks, lists or physics
l2-capstone.why: These are the advanced techniques Level 2 teaches.

options: A collection of work that shows your skill
l2-capstone.why: It is what you show people to demonstrate what you can do.

l2-capstone.stem: When presenting, you should be able to explain:
options: One clever piece of code and what was hardest
l2-capstone.why: Explaining your engineering decisions demonstrates real understanding.

l2-capstone.stem: Writing a spec before coding helps because:
l2-capstone.why: A defined target is what makes finishing possible.
